source.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
source.authors: Jing Huang; Atticus Geiger; Karel D'Oosterlinck; Zhengxuan Wu; Christopher Potts

record.tranche_reason: The study tests neuron-activation explanations in a language model with observational and causal evaluations, rather than measuring polysemanticity using the original vision-neuron examples or method.
record.gate_note: The study reports observational results about whether GPT-4 explanations predict neuron activations, including unexplained activation patterns. It also reports intervention results about causal efficacy, but those measure whether the explanation identifies causal mediators, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, so they are not rows here. Prompt examples and cited results are not recorded as findings.
record.test_reason: The paper audits GPT-4 explanations of GPT-2 XL MLP neurons. Appendix B directly asks whether unexplained activations (Type II errors) reflect several concepts encoded in one neuron. It reports that most such cases are activations on unrelated but coherent concepts. That is a result on V2 in a setting new relative to the originals. The main metrics (F1, precision, recall, IIA) measure explanation fidelity, not polysemanticity itself.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that even the most confident GPT-4 explanations of GPT-2 XL neurons have low observational fidelity (F1 0.56; precision 0.64, recall 0.50) and little or no causal efficacy. They argue that natural language is a poor explanation medium and that individual neurons are not the best unit of analysis. In Appendix B they add that most unexplained activations fall on unrelated coherent concepts, which they take as consistent with superposition-style polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates natural-language explanations against generated observational datasets and causal interchange interventions; it does not reproduce the original vision-neuron analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that results differ between observational and intervention evaluations, and that intervention effects increase when larger percentages of neurons are selected. These intervention results do not directly measure the versions catalogued here.

fits_no_version.finding: Neurons with explanations about one concept also activate strongly on its antonyms (at least 6 of 100 inspected Type II cases; the 'small/minor changes' neuron fires similarly on 'big/major').
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron explanations generated from top activations miss related or opposite senses that the neuron also responds to, so the neuron's true feature is broader than the explanation.

fits_no_version.finding: Intervening on single neurons never changed model behaviour causally; causal effects needed hundreds of neurons, and GPT-4 explanation-selected neurons performed about as well as random.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concepts in GPT-2 XL MLPs are causally distributed across many neurons rather than localized in single neurons.

record.peer_reviewed: BlackboxNLP Workshop on Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP
record.problems: The observational analysis samples only 300 of 1.7k neurons whose explanations scored at least 0.8, rather than estimating polysemanticity prevalence in the full model. Manual analysis is conditional on Type II errors. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The study notes that its findings are primarily about pre-trained GPT-2 XL and should not be construed as extending directly to other architectures.
record.rows_left_out: Intervention-based interchange-intervention accuracy results in Sections 4.3-4.4 and Tables 4 and 6 are left out because they measure causal efficacy of explanation-selected neuron sets, not responses to unrelated inputs. Probe-based F1 results in Table 1 are left out because they aggregate sets of neurons rather than measuring individual-neuron responses.

untested.parts: Share of all MLP neurons that are polysemantic, variation across layers, and other language models; only high-scoring neurons with Type II errors were inspected.
Superposition is invoked as an interpretation of the Type II errors but not tested.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not studied.
No comparison across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
Only a single anecdote (a days-of-week neuron firing on platforms after 'on') suggests a shared structure; there is no systematic test of whether unrelated mixtures are rare.
Activation-range choices are not varied systematically; only the contrast between GPT-4 simulation scoring and the authors' precision/recall is reported.

missing.what: F1 has a correlation of −0.1 with the GPT-4 score, and GPT-4 scoring (5 top plus 5 random examples) is insensitive to Type I errors. Whether a neuron looks monosemantically explained depends on the scoring and sampling method.

A days-of-week neuron also fires on 'Google'/'Facebook' when preceded by 'on'; its Type I errors are days not preceded by 'on'. This suggests a shared linguistic-structure feature behind apparently unrelated activations.
Form-based explanations have precision 0.78 versus 0.62 for the rest.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label for V2 was removed. It rested on untested parts (prevalence, layers), which belong under untested. R1 and R2 measure explanation fidelity and cannot separate polysemanticity from explanation vagueness. Only R3 bears directly on V2. The sample is restricted to the top-scoring 0.6% of neurons (300 of 1.7k with GPT-4 score ≥0.8), so no prevalence estimate is possible. The V7 label is text-based and modest: the paper shows scoring dependence for explanation quality, which bears on but is not identical to polysemanticity judgments. Tranche changed to T3 because polysemanticity is examined only as a side analysis of explanation errors, not with a method aimed at the claim.

versions.untested_parts: Vision models and the cited InceptionV1 neuron were not studied.
The study does not estimate the share of all MLP neurons that respond to unrelated inputs, compare that share across layers, or test other language models.
Superposition as the cause of mixed activations is discussed as a hypothesis, not directly tested.
Initialization, regularization, training noise, and capacity sufficiency are not tested as causes.
The study does not compare activation functions, architectures, or regularization regimes, or report performance costs of reducing polysemanticity.
The study finds some shared linguistic structures among activation patterns, but does not test whether apparently unrelated patterns share a feature that the network uses.
It does not systematically vary activation ranges examined or explanation-scoring methods to measure their effects on polysemanticity judgments.

rows.subject: GPT-2 XL
rows.operation_detail: Compared GPT-4 explanations with observed neuron activations on generated test sentences

conditions.value: 300 neurons (18%) sampled from 1.7k neurons with GPT-4 score at least 0.8

rows.measure: Mean F1 for explanation predictions of neuron activation
rows.note: The abstract and results also report precision 0.64 and recall 0.50. The result is for selected high-scoring explanations, not a population estimate of polysemantic-neuron prevalence.
rows.check: F1 combines precision (Type I errors, where the explanation over-predicts) with recall. Low F1 reflects explanation quality and vagueness as much as neurons responding to unrelated inputs. It cannot show the V2 effect, and the random-pairing baseline is not a polysemanticity baseline.

rows.subject: GPT-2 XL
rows.operation_detail: Measured recall of GPT-4 explanation predictions against neuron activations

conditions.value: 300 neurons (18%) sampled from 1.7k neurons with GPT-4 score at least 0.8

rows.note: The study defines recall over neuron activations; the low value is consistent with some activations not being captured by the proposed explanations, but is not a direct estimate of the share of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Recall 0.50 means half of the neuron's activating inputs fall outside the explanation. This conflates poor or vague explanations with genuinely unrelated responses. It is consistent with V2 but cannot by itself show unrelated responses or a share of neurons.

rows.subject: GPT-2 XL
rows.operation_detail: Manually inspected Type II error examples for activation on antonyms
rows.measure: Number of inspected cases involving antonyms of the explained concept
rows.note: Examples include activation on 'above' for an explanation about 'below', and on 'ended' for an explanation about continuation.
rows.check: Antonyms (e.g. 'above' for 'below') are semantically related, not unrelated inputs. This finding does not measure V2's polysemanticity; it reflects explanation error or a broader shared feature.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 XL MLP neurons with GPT-4 score ≥0.8 whose explanations had Type II errors (100 inspected)
relationships.reason: The majority of inspected Type II errors were activations on inputs unrelated to the explanation that formed coherent concepts, i.e. mixed concepts in single neurons (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Of 100 inspected Type II errors, most were activations on inputs unrelated to the explanation that themselves formed coherent concepts, pointing to mixed concepts within single neurons.
